outcomes.text: Evaluate laboratory, field and quasi experiments.
Evaluate structured, unstructured, naturalistic, controlled, participant, non-participant, overt and covert observations.
Evaluate questionnaires and structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews.
Explain how data are obtained for correlational analysis and distinguish positive, negative and no correlation.
Formulate research aims, questions, null and alternative hypotheses, one-tailed and two-tailed.
Distinguish target population and sample, and evaluate random, snowball, opportunity and self-selected sampling.
Evaluate repeated measures, independent measures and matched participants designs.
Identify and operationalise the IV and DV, and control extraneous variables.
Design observations with behavioural categories, coding frames, time sampling and event sampling.
Design self-reports with open and closed questions and Likert and semantic differential rating scales.

subtopics.title: Raw data and types of data

outcomes.text: Design and use raw data recording tables, using standard and decimal form and significant figures, and estimate from data.
Distinguish nominal, ordinal and interval data, quantitative and qualitative data, and primary and secondary data.
Calculate and interpret mode, median, mean, range, variance and standard deviation.
Use ratios, percentages, fractions and frequency tables.
Draw and interpret line graphs, pie charts, bar charts, histograms and scatter diagrams.
Interpret normal and skewed distribution curves, probability and significance levels.
Use statistical tables of critical values.
Choose parametric or specific non-parametric tests: Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, chi-square, binomial sign and Spearman's rho.
Explain type 1 and type 2 errors and use statistical symbols.
Evaluate representativeness and generalisability.
Distinguish internal, external, inter-rater, test-retest and split-half reliability.
Distinguish internal, face, construct, concurrent, criterion, external, population and ecological validity.
Explain demand characteristics, social desirability, researcher bias and researcher effects.
Apply the BPS Code of Ethics: respect, competence, responsibility and integrity.
Explain the purpose of each section of a practical report: abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, references and appendices.
Cite academic references using the Harvard system.
Explain the role of peer review in validating psychological knowledge.
Conduct and analyse small-scale self-report, observation, experiment and correlation practicals, with risk assessment.
Explain how society makes decisions about scientific issues and how psychology contributes to the economy and society.
Explain cause and effect, falsification, replicability and objectivity.
Explain induction, deduction and hypothesis testing.
Explain manipulation of variables, control, standardisation and quantifiable measurement.

Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.

Describe Simons and Chabris (1999) on visual inattention.
Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.
Describe Bandura et al. (1961) on transmission of aggression.
Describe Chaney et al. (2004), the Funhaler study.
Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.
Describe Kohlberg (1968) on stages of moral development.
Describe Lee et al. (1997) on evaluations of lying and truth-telling.
Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.
Describe Sperry (1968), the split brain study.
Describe Casey et al. (2011) on neural correlates of delay of gratification.
Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.
Describe Blakemore and Cooper (1970) on the impact of early visual experience.
Describe Maguire et al. (2000) on taxi drivers.
Compare the two studies and assess how the contemporary study changes understanding of the theme and of diversity.

topics.title: Section A: Evaluating the core studies

subtopics.title: Methodological issues in the core studies

outcomes.text: Compare strengths and weaknesses of the research methods and types of data used in the studies.
Evaluate the studies for ethics, validity, reliability, sampling bias and ethnocentrism.
Relate each core study to its key theme and its area of psychology.

topics.title: Section B: Areas, perspectives and debates

outcomes.text: Explain the principles, research, strengths, weaknesses and applications of the social, cognitive, developmental, biological and individual differences areas.
Compare each area with the others.
Explain the principles, research, strengths, weaknesses and applications of the behaviourist and psychodynamic perspectives.
Explain the debates: nature/nurture, freewill/determinism, reductionism/holism and individual/situational explanations.
Explain the debates: usefulness of research, ethics, socially sensitive research and psychology as a science.
Compare positions within each debate with applications and research evidence.

subtopics.title: Applying psychology to a novel source

outcomes.text: Recognise the psychological content in a novel source.
Make evidence-based suggestions in relation to the source.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of one's own suggestions.

topics.title: Section A: Issues in mental health

subtopics.title: History and definitions of mental health

outcomes.text: Explain historical views of mental illness, defining abnormality and categorising disorders.
Describe Rosenhan (1973), On being sane in insane places.
Describe the characteristics of an affective disorder, a psychotic disorder and an anxiety disorder.
Explain the biochemical, genetic and brain abnormality explanations of mental illness.
Describe Gottesman et al. (2010) on disorders in offspring of psychiatrically ill parents.
Describe a biological treatment of one specific disorder.
Explain the behaviourist and cognitive explanations of mental illness, and one of the humanistic, psychodynamic or cognitive neuroscience explanations.
Describe Szasz (2011), The myth of mental illness: 50 years later.
Describe a non-biological treatment of one specific disorder.
Explain intelligence and the biological factors affecting it, Van Leeuwen et al. (2008), and a method of assessing intelligence.
Explain pre-adult brain development and risk taking, Barkley-Levenson and Galván (2014), and a strategy to reduce risk taking.
Explain perceptual development, Gibson and Walk (1960), and a play strategy to develop perception.
Explain cognitive development and education, Wood et al. (1976), and a cognitive strategy to improve revision.
Explain development of attachment, Ainsworth and Bell (1970), and a strategy for an attachment friendly environment.
Explain the impact of advertising on children, Johnson and Young (2002), and a strategy to reduce its impact.
Explain what makes a criminal, Raine et al. (1997), and a biological strategy to prevent criminal behaviour.
Explain bias in collecting and processing forensic evidence, Hall and Player (2008), and a strategy to reduce it.
Explain collection of evidence, Memon and Higham (1999) on the cognitive interview, and a strategy for police interviews.
Explain psychology and the courtroom, Dixon et al. (2002), and a strategy to influence jury decision making.
Explain crime prevention, Wilson and Kelling (1982) on broken windows, and a prevention strategy.
Explain the effect of imprisonment, Haney et al. (1973), and a strategy to reduce reoffending.
Explain stressors in the environment, Black and Black (2007), and a strategy to manage environmental stress.
Explain biological rhythms, Czeisler et al. (1982), and a strategy to reduce jetlag or shift work effects.
Explain recycling and conservation behaviour, Lord (1994), and a technique to increase it.
Explain ergonomics and human factors, Drews and Doig (2014), and a workplace design based on ergonomic research.
Explain psychological effects of the built environment, Ulrich (1984), and a design to improve wellbeing.
Explain territory and personal space, Wells (2000), and an office design strategy.

topics.title: Section B: Sport and exercise psychology

outcomes.text: Explain arousal and anxiety in sport, Fazey and Hardy (1988), and a technique for managing them.
Explain exercise and mental health, Lewis et al. (2014), and an exercise strategy to improve mental health.
Explain motivation, self-efficacy and imagery, Munroe-Chandler et al. (2008), and a strategy to motivate athletes.
Explain personality and sport, Kroll and Crenshaw (1970), and a strategy to use personality knowledge.
Explain performing with others, teams and leadership, Smith et al. (1979), and a strategy to improve team performance.
Explain audience effects and home advantage, Zajonc et al. (1969), and a strategy for training for and playing spectator sports.

topics.title: Methodological issues and debates in applied psychology

subtopics.title: Issues and debates across applied topics

outcomes.text: Apply nature/nurture, freewill/determinism, reductionism/holism and individual/situational explanations to applied topics.
Apply usefulness of research, ethics, socially sensitive research and psychology as a science to applied topics.
Apply ethnocentrism, validity, reliability and sampling bias to applied research.
Apply background, key research and application to novel situations.
